name: Social Facts
statement: Ways of acting and thinking that exist outside us and constrain us are the true subject matter of sociology.
statementAccent: exist outside us and constrain us
meaning: Social facts are the central concept of the sociological method of Émile Durkheim, set out especially in his 1895 work The Rules of Sociological Method, which he used to establish sociology as a distinct science with its own subject matter. A social fact is a way of acting, thinking, or feeling that is external to the individual and that exerts a coercive power over them. In Durkheim's own definition, social facts consist of manners of acting, thinking, and feeling external to the individual, which are invested with a coercive power by virtue of which they exercise control over the individual. Social facts have three key characteristics: they are external to any particular individual, existing independently and often preceding and outliving them; they are coercive, constraining behavior and backed by sanctions ranging from social disapproval to legal punishment; and they are general or collective, widespread throughout a society rather than peculiar to one person. Examples include laws, morals, customs, language, money, religious beliefs, and institutions. Durkheim's guiding methodological rule was to treat social facts as things, studying them objectively and empirically like natural phenomena, and to explain social facts by other social facts rather than by individual psychology or biology. This established society as a reality in its own right and made sociology a distinct discipline.
mechanism: Durkheim defined social facts to carve out a subject matter that belongs to sociology and to no other science. A social fact is recognized by its two defining marks. First, it is external to the individual: it exists in the society at large, independent of any single person, and confronts each person as a given they did not create, since language, law, morality, and custom are already there when a person is born and remain after they die. Second, it is coercive: it constrains how people act, think, and feel, and its power is felt most clearly when one tries to resist it, because violations meet sanctions, whether the informal sanction of social disapproval or the formal sanction of legal punishment. Social facts are also general, shared across the society rather than idiosyncratic. From this definition Durkheim drew his key methodological principle: to treat social facts as things, meaning to study them from the outside, objectively and empirically, setting aside personal preconceptions, as a natural scientist studies natural objects. Crucially, he insisted that social facts must be explained by other social facts, not reduced to the psychology or biology of individuals, because society is a reality sui generis, of its own kind, that emerges from the association of individuals but is not reducible to them. This anti-reductionist stance gave sociology its own distinct object and method.

whyItMatters: The concept of social facts is foundational to sociology as a discipline, because it gave the new science a distinct subject matter and a rigorous method. By defining social facts as ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that are external to individuals and exert a coercive power over them, Émile Durkheim identified a domain of reality, society itself, that cannot be reduced to the psychology of individuals and that requires its own science to study. His insistence on treating social facts as things, studying them objectively and empirically like natural phenomena, established sociology as an autonomous, scientific discipline and provided a model for social research. The principle that social facts must be explained by other social facts, rather than by individual biology or psychology, is a cornerstone of sociological reasoning and a powerful statement of anti-reductionism, asserting that collective phenomena have their own reality and their own causes. The concept underlies the study of institutions, norms, culture, and social structure that defines much of sociology.

limits: The concept of social facts is foundational but reflects Durkheim's particular methodological program and has been debated. His insistence on treating social facts as external, coercive things and on explaining them only by other social facts is a strong anti-reductionist stance that stands in tension with approaches emphasizing individual meaning and agency, such as Max Weber's interpretive sociology, which seeks to understand the subjective meanings people attach to their action rather than treating social facts purely as external objects. Critics argue that treating social facts as things can understate how social phenomena are produced and reproduced through the interpretations and actions of individuals. The sharp separation of the social from the psychological has also been questioned. Durkheim's approach is thus one influential paradigm within sociology rather than the only one.
misreadings: Social facts are not merely individual habits or psychological states; they are external, coercive, and general ways of acting and thinking that belong to society and constrain individuals. Treating them as things does not mean they are physical objects, but that they should be studied objectively from the outside. And explaining social facts by other social facts is a methodological stance, not the only possible one, since interpretive sociology emphasizes individual meaning, so treating social facts as personal habits, as literally material, or as the sole valid approach, misreads Durkheim's foundational concept.
origin: The central concept of Émile Durkheim's method, set out in his 1895 work The Rules of Sociological Method, defining social facts as external, coercive, general ways of acting and thinking that are sociology's proper object of study.
